claims.text: Phase stability in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys is governed by competition between FCC solid-solution formation and BCC precipitation.
Alloy composition influences the competition between the two crystal structures.
The Al-to-other-elements ratio is a particularly important determinant of FCC versus BCC stability.
Annealing temperature and time influence FCC versus BCC phase formation.
Varying Al content and annealing conditions will alter the formation of FCC and BCC phases.
Optimizing Al content and annealing conditions will improve high-temperature strength.
Optimizing Al content and annealing conditions will improve environmental resistance.
Optimizing Al content and annealing conditions will improve radiation tolerance.
Optimizing Al content and annealing conditions will improve cryogenic toughness.
The optimized alloy will have a 20% higher yield strength than the baseline alloy.
The optimized alloy will have a 15% higher fracture toughness than the baseline alloy.
The baseline as-cast alloy has a yield strength of 800 MPa.
The baseline as-cast alloy has a fracture toughness of 100 MPa·m^(1/2).
The hypothesis is bounded to 5–20 at% Al, annealing temperatures of 500–1000°C, and annealing times of 1–10 hours.
The exact relationship among Al content, annealing conditions, and phase stability is not well understood.
Failure to obtain at least a 10% increase in both yield strength and fracture toughness under optimized conditions would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The prediction specifies 20% higher yield strength and 15% higher fracture toughness, but the falsification rule only requires 10% increases. Results between 10% and the predicted values would fail the stated prediction without falsifying the hypothesis.
